extracted.intended_audience: NIH applicants and peer reviewers (study section participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Official description of how NIH study sections assign reviewers, conduct pre-meeting scoring, run application discussions (order and process), calculate final scores, and the formal review criteria used in grant critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application assignment and reviewer roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each application is assigned to 3-4 reviewers (1 primary, 2 secondary, 1 reader). Assignment is based on expertise alignment and reviewers review for conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roles: primary prepares the main presentation and score, secondaries provide additional scored perspectives, reader reads but does not score. Assignments should match reviewer expertise to application content; COI checks occur at assignment and before discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary scoring and critique submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigned reviewers read each application thoroughly, write a critique summarizing strengths and weaknesses, and assign a preliminary Overall Impact score on a 1–9 scale prior to the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques and preliminary Overall Impact scores must be submitted in advance. Preliminary scores act as anchors in the review process and inform streamlining decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlining (Not Discussed) decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many review meetings use preliminary scores to determine which applications will be discussed in full; approximately the bottom 50% (in some sections, bottom 30–40%) are 'streamlined' and not discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlined applications still receive written critiques but no final overall impact score from the full panel. Streamlining decisions are made by reviewers (not the Scientific Review Officer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion order randomized
rubrics_metrics.description: The review order for discussed applications is randomized rather than ordered by preliminary overall impact scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization is intended to protect the integrity of the review process and reduce anchoring effects from early extreme scores or ordering biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI) recusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers who have a conflict of interest with a given application must leave the room (or virtual breakout) and do not participate in that application's discussion or scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COI recusal applies to both discussion and final scoring; only eligible (no-COI) panelists provide the final Overall Impact score for an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary reviewer presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary reviewer presents an approximately 3–5 minute summary of the application's strengths and weaknesses during the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary should succinctly synthesize the critique and highlight the key issues for panel discussion; clear, focused presentations influence the direction of the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary reviewers' contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary reviewer(s) add perspectives that may agree or disagree with the primary, emphasizing additional strengths or weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondaries should highlight complementary points and provide balanced commentary to inform the panel; differing viewpoints are expected and helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader role in discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader was assigned to read the application but not to score it; the reader provides additional perspective during discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader input can identify issues overlooked by assigned reviewers and helps the panel reach a fuller understanding of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open panel discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: After assigned reviewers present, all eligible panelists may comment during an open discussion of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open discussion is the forum for the panel to surface concerns, clarifying questions, and consensus-building. Comments from multiple panelists can shift perceptions and scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score range discussion prior to final scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary reviewer states a recommended score range during discussion; other panelists may revise their preliminary thinking based on the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating a score range helps calibrate the panel, but final scores are cast privately. Panelists should avoid unduly anchoring others when stating ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final scoring procedure and calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: All eligible panelists (those without COI) privately provide a final Overall Impact score for each discussed application; the final score equals the mean of eligible scores multiplied by 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final Overall Impact scores therefore range from 10 (high impact) through 90 (low impact). Percentile ranks are assigned and may vary by study section. Only eligible (no-COI) panelists' scores are averaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques must assess the significance of the proposed research by summarizing strengths and weaknesses related to the importance of the problem or barrier addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should evaluate whether the project addresses an important problem and the potential for impact; concrete examples of significance (or lack thereof) should be noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator(s) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques must evaluate the investigators' strengths and weaknesses, including expertise, experience, and appropriateness to carry out the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the PI's track record, team composition, and capability to execute the proposed plan; note concerns about training, leadership, or resource gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques must evaluate innovation by identifying strengths and weaknesses in the novelty of concepts, approaches, or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the project challenges current paradigms, introduces novel concepts or methods, or proposes incremental advances; distinguish true innovation from incremental changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques must assess the approach, including strengths and weaknesses of the study design, methodology, analyses, and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rigor, feasibility, statistical plans, potential pitfalls, contingency plans, and whether methods appropriately address aims; methodological flaws should be explicitly described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques must evaluate the research environment, detailing strengths and weaknesses of institutional support and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional facilities, collaborative environment, mentorship, and whether the environment contributes materially to project success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact (bottom-line assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each critique contains an Overall Impact statement summarizing the panel's bottom-line assessment of the project's likelihood to exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall Impact integrates strengths and weaknesses across criteria into a single assessment; reviewers use this to guide preliminary and final scoring (1–9 before conversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of Human Subjects criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicable, critiques must address strengths and weaknesses regarding the protection of human subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss adequacy of protections, risks, consent processes, and regulatory compliance; deficiencies should be identified and explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebrate animals criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicable, critiques must evaluate the use and welfare of vertebrate animals, noting strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess justification for animal use, appropriateness of species/models, and welfare measures; cite any ethical or regulatory concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource sharing plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques should address the adequacy of plans for resource sharing when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether data/materials will be shared appropriately and whether plans meet NIH expectations; note deficiencies or exemplary plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication of key biological resources
rubrics_metrics.description: When relevant, critiques should evaluate plans for authentication of key biological resources and note strengths/weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the application adequately describes authentication of reagents, cell lines, antibodies, etc., to ensure reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of oral discussion and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoken discussions in panels can shift scores significantly; strong primary reviewer advocacy can rescue borderline grants, and negative comments often resonate more than positive ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and applicants should recognize that in-meeting advocacy matters; panels should aim for balanced, evidence-based discussion to avoid undue influence from strong personalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score calibration and anchoring effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-meeting scores serve as anchors for discussion; discussion can move scores significantly and 'score creep' toward the middle is often observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should be aware of anchoring and mid-point drift; randomized order aims to mitigate order-based anchoring, but conscious calibration and justification of score changes is encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive biases to identify and mitigate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be aware of biases that influence outcomes, including status quo bias (favoring mainstream over innovative), confirmation bias, reviewer fatigue (later applications reviewed less thoroughly), and order effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and mitigate these biases by focusing on evidence, rotating reviewer roles where possible, and adhering to standardized criteria during evaluation.
